claim: Arm-amputation involves two powerful drivers for brain plasticity—sensory deprivation and altered use.
source: Arm-amputation involves two powerful drivers for brain plasticity—sensory deprivation and altered use.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the dual nature of plasticity drivers in amputation.

claim: Individuals with congenital or acquired limb-absence vary in whether they preferentially use their intact hand or residual arm in daily activities.
source: We report that individuals with congenital or acquired limb-absence vary in whether they preferentially use their intact hand or residual arm in daily activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral measurements from accelerometry and questionnaires presented in the study.

claim: The deprived sensorimotor cortex is employed by whichever limb individuals are over-using.
source: Using fMRI, we show that the deprived sensorimotor cortex is employed by whichever limb individuals are over-using.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing differential activation patterns in the deprived cortex based on limb usage.

claim: Individuals from either group that rely more on their intact hands showed increased intact hand representation in the deprived cortex, irrespective of the age at which deprivation occurred.
source: Individuals from either group that rely more on their intact hands (and report less frequent residual arm usage) showed increased intact hand representation in the deprived cortex, and increased white matter fractional anisotropy underlying the deprived cortex, irrespective of the age at which deprivation occurred.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI activation data and correlation analyses showing usage-dependent plasticity independent of deprivation age.

claim: Individuals from either group that rely more on their intact hands showed increased white matter fractional anisotropy underlying the deprived cortex, irrespective of the age at which deprivation occurred.
source: Individuals from either group that rely more on their intact hands (and report less frequent residual arm usage) showed increased intact hand representation in the deprived cortex, and increased white matter fractional anisotropy underlying the deprived cortex, irrespective of the age at which deprivation occurred.
evidence: This is supported by DTI data showing correlations between FA values and intact hand representation.

claim: Experience-driven plasticity in the human brain can transcend boundaries that have been thought to limit reorganisation after sensory deprivation in adults.
source: Our results demonstrate how experience-driven plasticity in the human brain can transcend boundaries that have been thought to limit reorganisation after sensory deprivation in adults.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that usage patterns, not just deprivation age, drive cortical reorganization.

claim: Loss of a hand makes simple tasks such as tying shoelaces a daily challenge, resulting in serious implications for quality of life and employment.
source: After losing a hand, simple tasks such as tying your shoelaces become a daily challenge, resulting in serious implications for quality of life and employment (Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jang et al., 2011.

claim: Adaptive plasticity is restricted in the adult primary sensory cortex following sensory deprivation, as shown recently in late blindness.
source: It has been thought that adaptive plasticity is restricted in the adult primary sensory cortex following sensory deprivation, as shown recently in late blindness (Baseler et al., 2011), suggesting limited scope for neurorehabilitation following sensory deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baseler et al., 2011.

claim: Most accounts of plasticity following arm amputation focused on sensory deprivation, and in particular on apparently passive remapping of adjacent face or arm representation into the deprived cortex.
source: Despite this, most accounts of plasticity following arm amputation focused on sensory deprivation, and in particular on apparently passive remapping of adjacent face or arm representation into the deprived cortex (Lotze et al., 1999; Ramachandran and Altschuler, 2009; Nava and Röder, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lotze et al., 1999; Ramachandran and Altschuler, 2009; Nava and Röder, 2011.

claim: Longer-range remapping has been reported, such as intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
source: Although longer-range remapping has also been reported, such as intact hand representation in the deprived cortex (Bogdanov et al., 2012), this is usually also explained as a passive result of inter-hemispheric dis-inhibition (Werhahn et al., 2002; Ramachandran and Altschuler, 2009; Simões et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bogdanov et al., 2012; Werhahn et al., 2002; Ramachandran and Altschuler, 2009; Simões et al., 2012.

claim: Previous accounts of plasticity following arm amputation ignore substantial adaptations in motor behaviour that accompany absence or loss of a limb, which could be powerful drivers for plasticity.
source: However, these accounts ignore substantial adaptations in motor behaviour that accompany absence or loss of a limb, which could be powerful drivers for plasticity (Scholz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scholz et al., 2009 and represents a critique of previous literature.

claim: Both congenital and acquired groups moved the intact hand more than the residual arm.
source: A laterality index, reflecting the relative number of movements performed by the intact hand vs the residual arm (Figure 1B), showed that both groups moved the intact hand more than the residual arm (t(7) = 3.48, p=0.01; t(11) = 10.60, p=0.001, one-sample t-test compared to zero for the congenital and acquired groups, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of accelerometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The acquired group exhibited stronger relative reliance on their intact hand compared to the congenital group.
source: We found that the acquired group exhibited stronger relative reliance on their intact hand, as demonstrated in a significantly greater lateralisation scores towards the intact hand, compared to the congenital group (t(18) = −2.67, p=0.016, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of laterality indices between groups shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Questionnaire ratings for residual arm usage were significantly greater for the congenital group compared with the acquired group.
source: Ratings were significantly greater for the congenital group (t(1,27) = 3.65, p=0.001), suggesting they use their residual arm more frequently in their daily routine, compared with the acquired group (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of questionnaire data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The group difference in residual arm usage remained significant after accounting for level of amputation and degree of functional and cosmetic prosthetic limb usage as covariates.
source: This group difference remained significant after accounting for level of amputation and degree of functional and cosmetic prosthetic limb usage as covariates (F(1,24) = 8.217, p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for potential confounds.

claim: Questionnaire ratings for residual arm usage were negatively correlated with the accelerometry-based laterality indices.
source: The questionnaire ratings for residual arm usage were negatively correlated with the accereometry-based laterality indices (r(18) = −0.53, p=0.012, Figure 1D), validating the questionnaires as a measurement of habitual usage strategies between the residual and intact limbs.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between two measurement methods shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Congenital 1-handed participants showed increased activation during residual arm movements compared with the acquired and control groups.
source: In line with their increased usage of the residual arm, congenital 1-handed participants showed increased activation during residual arm movements, compared with the other two groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cluster showing increased activation during residual arm movements in congenital participants was centred on the hand knob of the central sulcus of the deprived hemisphere, spanning both the pre- and the post-central gyri.
source: The resulting cluster showed two distinct local peaks of activation—in the anterior and posterior banks of the central sulcus (t = 3.73; x = 38, y = −20, z = 54 for the anterior peak and t = 3.93; x = 48, y = −20, z = 54 for the posterior peak, coordinates are based on the MNI 152 brain template).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data with specific anatomical coordinates.

claim: Acquired 1-handed participants showed significantly increased activation during intact hand movements compared to the congenital and control groups.
source: Conversely, acquired 1-handed participants, who displayed increased use of their intact hand, correspondingly showed significantly increased activation during intact hand movements compared to the other groups (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cluster showing increased activation during intact hand movements in acquired participants had a single peak, centred on the posterior bank of the central sulcus.
source: The resulting cluster had a single peak, centred on the posterior bank of the central sulcus (t = 5.24; x = 42, y = −18, z = 48 in MNI 152 space).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data with specific anatomical coordinates.

claim: The differential activation in both congenital and acquired groups was restricted to the hand area, as demonstrated by activation patterns in the control group.
source: Even though activations used to generate these two contrasts were measured during movements of different limbs (hand vs arm), and on different sides of the body (limbless side vs intact side), the differential activation was restricted in both cases to the hand area, as demonstrated by activation patterns in the control group (Figure 2A and inserts in Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with control group activation patterns shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Movements of a phantom limb elicit both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during imagined movement.
source: Recently, this phenomenology has been supported by empirical evidence demonstrating that movements of a phantom limb elicit both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during imagined movement (Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012.

claim: A significant interaction between groups and limbs was found in fMRI activation within the deprived cortex ROI.
source: A mixed effect analysis of variance showed a significant interaction between groups and limbs (F(2,47) = 3.67, p=0.033), reflecting dissociated recruitment of the deprived cortex by movements of the residual arm and intact hand in the two 1-handed groups (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ROI-based fMRI data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Congenital participants showed increased activation when moving their residual limb compared to acquired participants.
source: Post-hoc tests confirmed increased activation when congenital participants moved their (relatively over-used) residual limb, compared to acquired participants (Mann Whitney U = 6, n = 20, p=0.001) and compared to controls (t(30) = 2.37, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical tests of ROI-based fMRI data.

claim: Acquired participants showed greater activation within the deprived cortex when moving their intact hand compared to congenital participants and controls.
source: Similarly, greater activation within the deprived cortex was observed when acquired participants moved their (relatively over-used) intact hand, compared to congenital participants (t(26) = −3.68, p=0.001) and controls (t(37) = 2.96, p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical tests of ROI-based fMRI data.

claim: The results were independent of participant A07, who lost her hand at a young age.
source: These results were independent of participant A07, who lost her hand at a young age (t>2.81, p<0.008) (note that this participant was not included in the arm analysis above, due to her amputation level).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis excluding a specific participant.

claim: The difference between the two 1-handed groups was significant when accounting for level of amputation and degree of functional and cosmetic prosthetic limb usage.
source: The difference between the two 1-handed groups was also significant when accounting for level of amputation, and degree of functional and cosmetic prosthetic limb usage (F(1,15) = 11.357, p=0.004 and F(1,23) = 8.172, p=0.009 for residual arm and intact hand movements, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for potential confounds.

claim: For the congenital group, activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the contralateral residual arm was greater than activation in the homologous intact cortex during movements of the contralateral intact arm.
source: For the congenital group, activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the (contralateral) residual arm was greater than activation in the homolgous intact cortex during movements of the (contralateral) intact arm (t(1,9) = 2.45, p=0.037).
evidence: This is supported by within-group statistical comparison of fMRI activation shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the acquired group, activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the ipsilateral intact hand was greater than activation in the homologous intact cortex during movements of the ipsilateral phantom hand.
source: Similarly, for the acquired group, activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the (ipsilateral) intact hand was greater than activation in the homologous intact cortex during movements of the (ipsilateral) phantom hand (Makin et al., 2013) (t(1,16) = 3.08, p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by within-group statistical comparison of fMRI activation shown in Figure 4, with citation to Makin et al., 2013.

claim: The congenital group showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the intact hand compared to controls.
source: Specifically, the congenital group, who over-use the residual arm, showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the intact hand (t(31) = −2.61, p=0.014), whereas the acquired group, who over-use the intact hand, showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the residual arm (Mann Whitney U = 97, n = 39, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of ROI-based fMRI data.

claim: The acquired group showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the residual arm compared to controls.
source: Specifically, the congenital group, who over-use the residual arm, showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the intact hand (t(31) = −2.61, p=0.014), whereas the acquired group, who over-use the intact hand, showed reduced activation in the deprived cortex during movements of the residual arm (Mann Whitney U = 97, n = 39, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of ROI-based fMRI data.

claim: The reduced activation in 1-handed groups during movements of the limb not favoured for over-use potentially reflects a competitive relationship between the representations of the two limbs in the deprived cortex.
source: This result potentially reflects a competitive relationship between the representations of the two limbs in the deprived cortex in 1-handed individuals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: The deprived cerebellum showed increased activation in the congenital group during residual arm movements.
source: Similarly to the deprived cortex, the deprived cerebellum showed increased activation in the congenital group during residual arm movements (t(26) = −3.33, p=0.003), and increased activation in the acquired group during intact hand movement (t(18) = 2.75, p=0.013).
evidence: This is supported by ROI-based fMRI analysis of cerebellar activation.

claim: The deprived cerebellum showed increased activation in the acquired group during intact hand movement.
source: Similarly to the deprived cortex, the deprived cerebellum showed increased activation in the congenital group during residual arm movements (t(26) = −3.33, p=0.003), and increased activation in the acquired group during intact hand movement (t(18) = 2.75, p=0.013).
evidence: This is supported by ROI-based fMRI analysis of cerebellar activation.

claim: The patterns of altered representation identified in this study are not limited to reorganisation of body-part representations in the primary sensorimotor cortex.
source: This suggests that the patterns of altered representation identified in this study are not limited to reorganisation of body-part representations in the primary sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cerebellar findings.

claim: ROI-based comparisons between the acquired and control groups showed similar results when accounting for handedness.
source: ROI-based comparisons between the acquired and control groups were repeated as above, while accounting for handedness using this sub-group, with similar results (t(30) = 3.1, p=0.004 for increased representation during intact hand movements and t(37) = −2.25, p=0.032 for decreased residual arm representation during residual arm movements in acquired amputees vs controls).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for handedness.

claim: Within the acquired group, a trend for a correlation between chronic phantom pain scores and usage was found, such that individuals with worst chronic pain tend to use their residual arm less.
source: Indeed, within the acquired group a trend for a correlation between chronic phantom pain scores and usage was found (r(16) = −0.40, p=0.099), such that individuals with worst chronic pain tend to use their residual arm less.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between pain and usage measures.

claim: Increased activation was maintained in the congenital group during residual arm movements when chronic phantom pain ratings were included as a covariate.
source: Increased activation was maintained both in the congenital group (relative to the acquired group) during residual arm movements (F(1,19) = 12.57, p=0.002) and in the acquired group (relative to the congenital group) during intact hand movements (F(1,27) = 6.10, p=0.021).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for phantom pain.

claim: Increased activation was maintained in the acquired group during intact hand movements when chronic phantom pain ratings were included as a covariate.
source: Increased activation was maintained both in the congenital group (relative to the acquired group) during residual arm movements (F(1,19) = 12.57, p=0.002) and in the acquired group (relative to the congenital group) during intact hand movements (F(1,27) = 6.10, p=0.021).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis controlling for phantom pain.

claim: The activation patterns are not merely epiphenomenal to phantom pain.
source: These results suggest that the activation patterns presented above are not merely epiphenomenal to phantom pain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis controlling for phantom pain.

claim: Greater usage of the residual arm was associated with less activation during intact hand movements in the deprived cortex.
source: Indeed, when considering usage across both 1-handed groups we found that greater usage of the residual arm was associated with less activation during intact hand movements in the deprived cortex (r(26) = −0.43, p=0.021), even when accounting for age of sensory deprivation (r(25) = −0.36, p=0.032).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The correlation between residual arm usage and intact hand activation in the deprived cortex remained significant when accounting for age of sensory deprivation.
source: Indeed, when considering usage across both 1-handed groups we found that greater usage of the residual arm was associated with less activation during intact hand movements in the deprived cortex (r(26) = −0.43, p=0.021), even when accounting for age of sensory deprivation (r(25) = −0.36, p=0.032).
evidence: This is supported by partial correlation analysis controlling for deprivation age.

claim: The correlation between residual arm usage and intact hand activation was strengthened when only considering prosthetic limb users.
source: This effect was strengthened when repeating the same partial correlation while only considering the prosthetic limb users (r(19) = −0.61, p=0.003 and r(18) = −0.56, p=0.005, respectively), suggesting that rehabilitation may strengthen the relationship between adaptive plasticity and usage, however further research will be required to identify the relationship between prosthesis usage and adaptive brain plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis in a subset of participants.

claim: Rehabilitation may strengthen the relationship between adaptive plasticity and usage.
source: This effect was strengthened when repeating the same partial correlation while only considering the prosthetic limb users (r(19) = −0.61, p=0.003 and r(18) = −0.56, p=0.005, respectively), suggesting that rehabilitation may strengthen the relationship between adaptive plasticity and usage, however further research will be required to identify the relationship between prosthesis usage and adaptive brain plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the stronger correlation in prosthesis users.

claim: No significant differences in FA were found between the three groups.
source: No significant differences in FA were found between the three groups, suggesting that deprivation in itself may be insufficient to induce significant white matter change (although see Langer et al. (2012) for a study showing reduced FA in the corticospinal tract following several weeks of arm immobilisation).
evidence: This is supported by DTI analysis comparing groups.

claim: Deprivation in itself may be insufficient to induce significant white matter change.
source: No significant differences in FA were found between the three groups, suggesting that deprivation in itself may be insufficient to induce significant white matter change (although see Langer et al. (2012) for a study showing reduced FA in the corticospinal tract following several weeks of arm immobilisation).
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of group differences in FA, with citation to Langer et al. (2012) for context.

claim: Across both 1-handed groups, individuals showing greater activation in the deprived cortex during intact hand movements had higher FA values in the corticospinal tract and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus in the deprived hemisphere.
source: However, across both 1-handed groups, individuals showing greater activation in the deprived cortex during intact hand movements had higher FA values in the corticospinal tract and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFO) in the deprived hemisphere (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by voxel-wise correlation analysis of DTI data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant correlations were identified between FA and degree of activation in the deprived cortex during residual arm movements.
source: No significant correlations were identified between FA and degree of activation in the deprived cortex during residual arm movements.
evidence: This is a negative finding from DTI correlation analysis.

claim: This is the first evidence that altered patterns of adaptive limb use in individuals with unilateral hand absence are reflected in distinct patterns of cortical reorganization.
source: We provide the first evidence that altered patterns of adaptive limb use, in individuals with unilateral hand absence, are reflected in distinct patterns of cortical reorganization.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: This is the first detailed description of patterns of daily limb usage in individuals with congenital and acquired limb-loss using physiological measurements.
source: Using physiological measurements, we provide the first detailed description of patterns of daily limb usage in individuals with congenital and acquired limb-loss.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty of the behavioral measurements.

claim: Representation patterns in the deprived cortex of 1-handed individuals are contingent upon the limb-use strategy adopted by individuals, rather than a sensitive period in development.
source: Next, using fMRI we show that representation patterns in the deprived cortex of 1-handed individuals are contingent upon the limb-use strategy adopted by individuals, rather than a sensitive period in development: Individuals from either 1-handed group that rely more on their intact hands showed increased representation of the (ipsilateral) intact hand in the deprived cortex, irrespective of age at deprivation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings showing usage-dependent plasticity independent of deprivation age.

claim: 69% of individuals with limb loss have to change job or become unemployed.
source: As a result of limb loss, 69% of sufferers have to change job or become unemployed (Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jang et al., 2011.

claim: How best to rehabilitate individuals with limb loss and allow them to return to active and productive lifestyles is unknown.
source: How best to rehabilitate these individuals, and allow them to return to active and productive lifestyles, is unknown (Nimhurchadha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nimhurchadha et al., 2013.

claim: A relatively large number of individuals do not use prosthetic limbs and prefer to carry out daily activities with their intact hand.
source: While tremendous resources are dedicated to aiding 1-handed populations through the development of sophisticated prosthetic limbs (Kuiken et al., 2009), a relatively large number of the individuals do not use them and prefer to carry out daily activities with their intact hand (Jang et al., 2011; Østlie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuiken et al., 2009; Jang et al., 2011; Østlie et al., 2012.

claim: Different individuals adapt to limblessness in varying ways, with some relying on the intact limb and others showing remarkable ability with their residual limb or a prosthetic limb.
source: Clinicians are aware that different individuals adapt to limblessness in varying ways–with some relying on the intact limb (Jones and Davidson, 1999) and others showing remarkable ability with their residual limb or a prosthetic limb (Smurr et al., 2008; Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jones and Davidson, 1999; Smurr et al., 2008; Jang et al., 2011.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, there has been no previous empirical study of the range of adaptive motor behaviours taken in 1-handed individuals in their natural environment.
source: Surprisingly, however, to our knowledge there has been no previous empirical study of the range of adaptive motor behaviours taken in 1-handed individuals in their natural environment (Lindner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study, with citation to Lindner et al., 2010.

claim: Previous studies of maladaptive brain changes after amputation have been instrumental in guiding new evidence-based rehabilitation interventions to treat phantom pain.
source: Previous studies of maladaptive brain changes after amputation (Flor et al., 1995) have been instrumental in guiding new evidence-based rehabilitation interventions to treat phantom pain (Chan et al., 2007; Lotze et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flor et al., 1995; Chan et al., 2007; Lotze et al., 1999.

claim: The study of brain changes after amputation has not previously been brought to bear on the clinical problem of adaptive motor behaviour.
source: However, the study of brain changes after amputation has not previously been brought to bear on the clinical problem of adaptive motor behaviour.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's focus.

claim: Understanding the scope for adult human brain plasticity is a key consideration for designing successful future neurorehabilitation approaches.
source: Understanding the scope for adult human brain plasticity is a key consideration for designing successful future neurorehabilitation approaches (Krakauer, 2006; Koenig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krakauer, 2006; Koenig et al., 2013.

claim: Patterns of increased representation of displaced body parts in the deprived cortex closely relate to adaptive daily strategies of limb-usage in individuals with upper limb absence.
source: We found that patterns of increased representation of displaced body parts in the deprived cortex closely relate to adaptive daily strategies of limb-usage in individuals with upper limb absence: people with congenital hand absence, who are better at incorporating their residual arms in daily tasks, activate their missing hand cortex during residual arm movements (Figures 2B, 3B, 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data in Figures 2B, 3B, and 4.

claim: People with congenital hand absence, who are better at incorporating their residual arms in daily tasks, activate their missing hand cortex during residual arm movements.
source: We found that patterns of increased representation of displaced body parts in the deprived cortex closely relate to adaptive daily strategies of limb-usage in individuals with upper limb absence: people with congenital hand absence, who are better at incorporating their residual arms in daily tasks, activate their missing hand cortex during residual arm movements (Figures 2B, 3B, 4).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figures 2B, 3B, and 4.

claim: The finding of residual arm activation in the deprived cortex in congenital participants is consistent with previous reports of reorganisation associated with compensatory foot-use in individuals with bilateral congenital upper limb malformation.
source: This is consistent with previous reports of reorganisation associated with compensatory foot-use in individuals with bilateral congenital upper limb malformation (Stoeckel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stoeckel et al., 2009.

claim: 1-handed individuals with acquired amputation, who are more dependent on their intact hands for daily activities, show strong activation in their deprived cortex when the intact hand is moving.
source: Conversely, the 1-handed individuals with acquired amputation, who are more dependent on their intact hands for daily activities, show strong activation in their deprived cortex when the intact hand is moving (Figures 2C, 3C, 4).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figures 2C, 3C, and 4.

claim: The dissociative representation between congenital and acquired groups doesn't exclusively rely on the cause of or age at deprivation.
source: However, this dissociative representation doesn't exclusively rely on the cause of or age at deprivation: increased ipsilateral intact hand representation was associated with the usage strategy adopted by individuals (Figure 3D), such that people who have learned to incorporate their residual arms in daily tasks tended to show reduced intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: People who have learned to incorporate their residual arms in daily tasks tended to show reduced intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
source: However, this dissociative representation doesn't exclusively rely on the cause of or age at deprivation: increased ipsilateral intact hand representation was associated with the usage strategy adopted by individuals (Figure 3D), such that people who have learned to incorporate their residual arms in daily tasks tended to show reduced intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: It is possible that adaptive strategies for compensatory limb-usage drive similar, yet subtler differences in other brain areas underlying limb usage.
source: However, it is possible that adaptive strategies for compensatory limb-usage drive similar, yet subtler differences in other brain areas underlying limb usage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential broader effects.

claim: Habitual usage strategies could produce further changes in brain representation beyond the deprived cortex and even the sensorimotor system.
source: We therefore cannot rule out the possibility that habitual usage strategies could produce further changes in brain representation, beyond the deprived cortex and even the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential broader effects.

claim: The IFO has been recently implicated in visuospatial representation, as well as visuomotor control.
source: The IFO has been recently implicated in visuospatial representation, as well as visuomotor control (Urbanski et al., 2008; Migliaccio et al., 2012), which may be relevant for lateralised limb usage (Makin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Urbanski et al., 2008; Migliaccio et al., 2012; Makin et al., 2010.

claim: The structural differences in the corticospinal tract associated with increased representation of the intact hand in the deprived cortex may shed new light on the origin of bimanual plasticity in amputees.
source: The structural differences in the corticospinal tract, associated with increased representation of the intact hand in the deprived cortex, may shed new light on the origin of bimanual plasticity in amputees, which has previously been regarded as a consequence of reduced inter-hemispheric inhibition (Simões et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the DTI findings, with citation to Simões et al., 2012.

claim: Similar results were found in the deprived cerebellum as identified in the sensorimotor cortex, despite fundamental differences in body-part topography in these two brain regions.
source: Indeed, we find similar results in the deprived cerebellum, as identified in the sensorimotor cortex, despite fundamental differences in body-part topography (Shambes et al., 1978) in these two brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by the cerebellar ROI analysis, with citation to Shambes et al., 1978.

claim: One tentative interpretation is that longer-range plasticity (where the deprived cortex is recruited by the intact hand) elicits structural white matter change, whereas more local plasticity (where the deprived cortex is recruited by the residual arm) does not.
source: One tentative interpretation of these findings is that longer-range plasticity (where the deprived cortex is recruited by the intact hand) elicits structural white matter change, whereas more local plasticity (where the deprived cortex is recruited by the residual arm) does not.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential DTI findings.

claim: The cross-sectional nature of the study does not allow differentiation between experience-dependent and pre-existing variations in white matter structure that might confer a bias towards intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
source: However, the cross-sectional nature of the study does not allow us to differentiate between experience-dependent and pre-existing variations in white matter structure that might confer a bias towards intact hand representation in the deprived cortex.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study design.

claim: Adaptive limb usage strategies serve as powerful drivers of both functional and structural plasticity in adults.
source: To conclude, we demonstrate how adaptive limb usage strategies may serve as powerful drivers of both functional and structural plasticity in adults.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fMRI and DTI findings.

claim: The deprived cortex in people with either congenital or acquired hand absence is employed by whichever part of the upper limb individuals are relatively over-using to compensate for their disability.
source: We show that the deprived cortex in people with either congenital or acquired hand absence is employed by whichever part of the upper limb individuals are relatively over-using (compared to other 1-handed individuals) to compensate for their disability.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The recruitment of the deprived cortex by the over-used limb occurs irrespective of whether this is a hand or an arm and the degree to which it is typically represented in the deprived brain area.
source: This occurs irrespective of whether this is a hand or an arm and the degree to which it is typically represented in the deprived brain area.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing usage-dependent plasticity across different body parts.

claim: Adaptive plasticity in amputees transcends the boundaries thought to restrict reorganisation after sensory deprivation in the adult human brain.
source: By demonstrating that adaptive plasticity in amputees transcends the boundaries thought to restrict reorganisation after sensory deprivation in the adult human brain, our results may inspire future research, aimed at utilising neurorehabilitation to improve usage of both residual and intact arms, as well as artificial arms, in 1-handed individuals of all ages.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: The results may inspire future research aimed at utilising neurorehabilitation to improve usage of both residual and intact arms, as well as artificial arms, in 1-handed individuals of all ages.
source: By demonstrating that adaptive plasticity in amputees transcends the boundaries thought to restrict reorganisation after sensory deprivation in the adult human brain, our results may inspire future research, aimed at utilising neurorehabilitation to improve usage of both residual and intact arms, as well as artificial arms, in 1-handed individuals of all ages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: 18 individuals with sustained unilateral upper limb amputation (mean age ± s.e.m = 46 ± 3, 6 with absent right hand) were recruited for the study.
source: 18 individuals with sustained unilateral upper limb amputation (mean age ± s.e.m = 46 ± 3, 6 with absent right hand), 11 individuals with a congenital unilateral upper limb deficit (age = 35 ± 4, 3 with absent right hand) and 22 intact controls (age = 41 ± 3, 7 left hand dominant) were recruited for the study (see Table 1 for demographic details).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

source: 18 individuals with sustained unilateral upper limb amputation (mean age ± s.e.m = 46 ± 3, 6 with absent right hand), 11 individuals with a congenital unilateral upper limb deficit (age = 35 ± 4, 3 with absent right hand) and 22 intact controls (age = 41 ± 3, 7 left hand dominant) were recruited for the study (see Table 1 for demographic details).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

source: 18 individuals with sustained unilateral upper limb amputation (mean age ± s.e.m = 46 ± 3, 6 with absent right hand), 11 individuals with a congenital unilateral upper limb deficit (age = 35 ± 4, 3 with absent right hand) and 22 intact controls (age = 41 ± 3, 7 left hand dominant) were recruited for the study (see Table 1 for demographic details).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Data from one individual with acquired deprivation and one control were discarded due to excessive head movements during fMRI and problems during DTI data acquisition.
source: Data from one individual with acquired deprivation and one control were discarded, due to excessive head movements (>3 mm) during fMRI and problems during DTI data acquisition (respectively).
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria.

claim: The questionnaire was modified to accommodate participants with various levels of deprivation while considering the unique confounds of unilateral amputees.
source: As previous motor activity logs were designed to assess mobility of a paralyzed hand, the questionnaire was modified while considering the unique confounds of unilateral amputees (Lindner et al., 2010), and was aimed to accommodate participants with various levels of deprivation.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology with citation to Lindner et al., 2010.

claim: Data for each of the three movement axes was initially smoothed using a 500 ms kernel to discard high frequency noise.
source: Data for each of the three movement axes was initially smoothed using a 500 ms kernel, to discard high frequency noise.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: Movements were identified as difference in acceleration that was above a threshold of 0.2 m/s2 in at least one axis.
source: In each time window, movements were identified as difference in acceleration that was above a threshold of 0.2 m/s2 in at least one axis, provided that this increase was preceded and followed by periods of no movement (a difference between maximal and minimal acceleration below 0.2 m/s2) in all axes.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Data collected for individuals with absent right hands were mirror reversed across the mid-sagittal plane prior to all analyses.
source: Data collected for individuals with absent right hands (6 acquired and 3 congenital participants), were mirror reversed across the mid-sagittal plane prior to all analyses so that the hemisphere corresponding to the missing hand was consistently aligned.
evidence: This is a description of the data preprocessing methodology.

claim: Data collected for left-hand dominant controls were also flipped to account for potential biases stemming from the mirror reversal procedure.
source: Data collected for left-hand dominant controls (n = 7) were also flipped, in order to account for potential biases stemming from this procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the data preprocessing methodology.
